mainEntity.name: Can I have an MRI if I have metal dental crowns?

acceptedAnswer.text: In the majority of cases, yes. Metal dental crowns made from commonly used dental alloys are generally considered safe for MRI scanning. Most dental alloys are non-ferromagnetic, meaning they are not significantly attracted to the MRI's magnetic field. You should always disclose your dental restorations during the MRI pre-assessment process, as the radiology team will factor this into the scanning plan. In some cases involving head or neck imaging, the team may note potential image distortion near the dental metalwork.

mainEntity.name: Will my metal crown affect the quality of the MRI image?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is possible that a metal crown may cause a degree of image distortion — known as a susceptibility artefact — in the area immediately surrounding the restoration. This is more likely to be relevant if the MRI is focused on the head, jaw, or neck region. For scans of other body areas such as the spine, abdomen, or limbs, dental crowns are unlikely to have any meaningful effect on image quality. Your radiographer will assess this based on the specific scan required.

mainEntity.name: Should I remove a removable dental appliance before an MRI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. If you have removable dental appliances such as partial dentures with metal clasps, orthodontic retainers, or temporary crowns that are not definitively cemented, you will typically be asked to remove these before entering the MRI room. Fixed crowns, bridges, and implants cannot be removed and are assessed as part of the pre-screening process. Always inform the MRI team of both fixed and removable dental appliances.

mainEntity.name: Are porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns treated the same as all-metal crowns for MRI purposes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crowns have a metal substructure beneath the ceramic outer layer. The metallic component is assessed in the same way as an all-metal crown for MRI purposes. The specific alloy used in the substructure will influence how the crown interacts with the magnetic field. If you are unsure of the materials in your PFM crown, your dental practice may be able to provide this information from your clinical records.

mainEntity.name: Can a metal dental crown move during an MRI?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is an understandable concern, but for dental crowns made from standard dental alloys, movement during an MRI is not a clinically expected outcome. Because these materials are non-ferromagnetic or only very weakly magnetic, the magnetic force acting upon them is negligible. The crown is also cemented firmly onto the tooth structure, which provides additional physical retention. If you have concerns about a specific crown — particularly an older or unfamiliar restoration — speaking to your dentist before your scan is a sensible step.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a letter from my dentist before having an MRI with a dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is not routinely required for standard metal dental crowns. In most cases, disclosing your dental restorations during the MRI pre-assessment questionnaire is sufficient. However, if your medical or radiology team requests written documentation — for example, if you have extensive dental metalwork, implants, or if the scan is particularly close to the jaw region — your dental practice should be able to provide a brief letter confirming the type of restoration and materials used. Contact your dental team well in advance of your appointment if documentation is needed.
